articles.title: How a 5,000-Design Database Changes DFM Review and First-Shot Success
articles.excerpt: Most mold shops treat design for manufacturability as a checklist. We treat it as a search problem. After 23 years and more than 2,000 molds a year, the most valuable asset in our toolroom is not a ma…
articles.body: Most mold shops treat design for manufacturability as a checklist. We treat it as a search problem. After 23 years and more than 2,000 molds a year, the most valuable asset in our toolroom is not a machine — it is a database of over 5,000 mold designs with their outcomes attached. The practical effect is that a new program rarely starts from zero. What the database actually contains Each entry records the part geometry, the mold configuration, the steel choice, the gate and runner strategy, the cycle time achieved and — most importantly — what went wrong at T1 and how it was fixed. That last field is what turns a CAD archive into a decision tool. When a customer sends a STEP or IGES file, our engineers search for the closest prior geometry before they quote.

articles.title: A video labelled 60 fps averaged 30.68: timestamps decide when a frame shows
articles.excerpt: A frame does not play at "frame number divided by fps". It plays at the timestamp stored with it, called the PTS. One clip makes the point: its label said 60 fps, its frames averaged 30.68 fps. Here i…
articles.body: A frame does not play at "frame number divided by fps". It plays at the timestamp stored with it, called the PTS. One clip makes the point: its label said 60 fps, its frames averaged 30.68 fps. Here is the mental model first, before any ffmpeg flag. The numbers come from two small test clips on one Apple-silicon Mac, one run each. The first is a synthetic 20-second clip generated with deliberately uneven frame times. The second is a canvas animation recorded with MediaRecorder in a desktop browser. They cover these two files only, so don't stretch them to phone videos, which were not tested. What a file stores for each frame It is easy to picture a video as a pile of pictures plus one number, the fps.

articles.title: Data Brokers - The Business of Trading Personal Information.
articles.excerpt: Who knows more about you than your friends, colleagues - and sometimes even you do? Perhaps a company you have never heard of. It may know where you live, what you buy, which websites you visit, and w…
articles.body: Who knows more about you than your friends, colleagues - and sometimes even you do? Perhaps a company you have never heard of. It may know where you live, what you buy, which websites you visit, and what interests you. Companies like these are known as data brokers. Their business is built on collecting, combining, and selling information about people. Their sources include apps, websites, loyalty programs, purchases, public records, and data obtained from other companies. Sometimes people provide information themselves when filling out forms or agreeing to a service’s terms and conditions. Other information is collected automatically, for example, through advertising identifiers, cookies, and tracking technologies.

articles.title: The skills effect transfers: 20 of 24 model–harness pairs on a second benchmark — and one experimental arm still missing
articles.excerpt: The skills effect transfers: 20 of 24 model–harness pairs on a second benchmark — and one experimental arm still missing Under our last autopsy, a commenter asked for the test we hadn't run: does the…
articles.body: The skills effect transfers: 20 of 24 model–harness pairs on a second benchmark — and one experimental arm still missing Under our last autopsy, a commenter asked for the test we hadn't run: does the scaffold effect hold on a *different benchmark, or was it one dataset's quirk? This post is that test — including a result that surprised us.* Last week we pulled 7,224 public ClawsBench trials apart and found that the benchmark's scaffold was really one variable: a one-page meta prompt carried the entire +39–56 point lift, and a curated skills library added zero measurable points on top of it. A commenter (reidmarlow, who has been right before) pushed on exactly the right weakness: that decomposition came from one benchmark, and a null result is not proof of equivalence.

articles.body: You add two seconds to a storyboard shot so the audience can see a clue. Suddenly the dialogue in the next shot starts before the clue appears. Fixing one timing mistake by hand is easy. Across several episodes, keeping the scratch audio aligned with revised panels becomes a bookkeeping problem. A small Python script can calculate the new cue times from a list of panel durations. Use these times to reposition the temporary dialogue in your editor. The script leaves the audio files untouched, so you keep control over the actual cut. Start with the action that triggers the line Imagine a short drama set in an upholstery shop. articles.title: Part 4: Fighting FastAPI Quirks (And Winning!)
articles.excerpt: Welcome to Part 4 of building a real-time data API that AI agents can pay for with USDC micropayments via the x402 protocol. This week was less about shipping features and more about wrestling with Fa…
articles.body: Welcome to Part 4 of building a real-time data API that AI agents can pay for with USDC micropayments via the x402 protocol. This week was less about shipping features and more about wrestling with FastAPI’s opinionated defaults. I’m not a FastAPI expert, so a couple of its “helpful” behaviors caused real friction with the strict requirements of x402. Here’s what broke, why it broke, and how I fixed it. Quirk #1: The Dreaded "detail" Wrapper The x402 protocol is strict. When an agent hits an unpaid endpoint, you must return HTTP 402 with a JSON body whose root keys match the challenge format exactly (typically accepts , resource , and related fields). No wrapping allowed.

articles.body: One of Grand Theft Auto 6 ’s strangest random encounters occurs when you’re offering taxi services, and a man with a beard wearing a dark suit and sunglasses climbs into the backseat with a gun. This can happen if you’re playing as either Jason or Lucia, but both scenes play out the same way: The man wants you to run a red light, ignore phone calls, and drive him to Harborside Park in Vice Beach. He also sounds an awful lot like Tom Cruise, with a calm but forceful demeanor that seems almost sociopathic . articles.title: NASA Awards Contract for NOAA’s Near Earth Orbit Network Program
articles.excerpt: NASA, on behalf of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), has awarded a contract to Northrop Grumman Systems Corporation for the Sounder for Microwave-Based Applications (SMBA) in…
articles.body: Credit: NASA NASA, on behalf of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), has awarded a contract to Northrop Grumman Systems Corporation for the Sounder for Microwave-Based Applications (SMBA) instruments on NOAA’s Near Earth Orbit Network (NEON) satellites. The cost-plus-fixed-fee, firm-fixed-price, and time-and-materials hybrid contract has a value of $290.6 million. The period of performance runs from Nov. 23 through April 1, 2042. The work will take place at the awardee’s facility. Under the contract, Northrop Grumman will provide the design, development, production, testing, and mission support for three SMBA instruments, the next generation of low Earth orbit microwave sounders.

articles.title: How sci‑fi imagines sports in microgravity, and how zero‑g sports might actually work
articles.excerpt: How realistic are the zero-g sports we see in sci-fi? We talk to Les Johnson, former Chief Technologist for NASA, to find out.
articles.body: Sports in space have a long and proud tradition, whether it's Alan Shepard playing golf on the moon or the crew of the ISS hosting their own version of the Summer Olympics . The future looks bright as well, with the foundation of the Space Games Federation , the self-described "first governing and sanctioning body for competitive sports played in zero or micro-gravity," co-founded by a NASA astronaut. Not to be outdone, science fiction has expanded the idea of zero-g and low-gravity sports to their logical extent, imagining everything from Doctor Who's zero-g squash to the advanced, gamified combat simulations of Ender's Game.
